Sure thing. A useful way of visualizing biodiversity is with principal component analysis. PCA is a mathematical procedure that uses an orthogonal transformation to convert a set of observations of possibly correlated variables into a set of values of uncorrelated variables called principal components. In biology, it is used to discover how different a pair of individuals of one population is from a pair from another. Ultimately, the answer depends on the number of polymorphisms used to define the dissimilarity and the populations being compared.

This PCA plot takes a large sampling of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) of many individuals across the globe, narrowed down to what we would call “caucasoids.” In this instance, nucleotides are the four molecules–A, T, G, C–which pair in a strand of DNA. An SNP is a single variation in the pairing within a single strand of DNA. This can be used to determine genetic distance. You will notice an overall clustering pattern by which we can identify individuals and their respective populations and races.
